## Purpose

This SOP describes the field and office procedures for conducting a
wetland delineation using the three-parameter approach established by
the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE). A jurisdictional wetland must
exhibit all three criteria simultaneously: hydrophytic vegetation,
hydric soils, and wetland hydrology [@usace1987]. Delineation
establishes the boundary between jurisdictional wetlands (and other
waters of the US) and upland areas, which is a prerequisite for
regulatory compliance under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act.

Wetland delineation at EA Program sites supports baseline
characterization, impact assessment, restoration planning, and student
training in applied environmental science.


## Scope

- **Applies to:** Freshwater palustrine wetlands (marshes, swamps,
  riparian wetlands, vernal pools, seeps) at EA Program field sites in
  the Arid West region of California. This SOP follows the USACE Arid
  West Regional Supplement [@usace2010regional], which supersedes the
  1987 Manual for all delineations in this region.
- **Does not apply to:** Tidal or estuarine wetlands (require separate
  tidal methods); riverine waters regulated solely as ordinary high
  water mark (OHWM) features; non-USACE state-level wetland
  determinations under California law (e.g., Porter-Cologne Act), which
  may apply different criteria.
- **Location:** All EA Program wetland field sites


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                              |
|:------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve delineation design; coordinate permits and landowner access |
| Trained Personnel | Conduct three-parameter assessment per this SOP             |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent plot assessment        |


## Definitions

- **Dominant species:** A species contributing 50% or more of the
  relative frequency or relative cover within a stratum; used in the
  50/20 rule for hydrophytic vegetation determination.
- **Facultative (FAC):** A wetland indicator status category applied
  to plant species that occur in both wetland and upland habitats with
  roughly equal frequency (34--66% occurrence in wetlands); neither
  confirms nor denies wetland conditions when dominant.
- **Facultative upland (FACU):** Plants that usually occur in uplands
  (67--99% upland occurrence) but are occasionally found in wetlands;
  their dominance is evidence against hydrophytic vegetation.
- **Facultative wetland (FACW):** Plants that usually occur in wetlands
  (67--99% wetland occurrence); their dominance is strong evidence for
  hydrophytic vegetation.
- **Hydric soil:** A soil that formed under conditions of saturation,
  flooding, or ponding long enough to develop anaerobic conditions in
  the upper part; identified by USACE hydric soil field indicators
  (e.g., depleted matrix, redox concentrations, sulfidic odor); a
  required criterion for wetland delineation [@usace1987].
- **Hydrophytic vegetation:** Plant community dominated (by the 50/20
  rule) by species with a wetland indicator status of OBL, FACW, or FAC;
  a required criterion for wetland delineation.
- **Obligate wetland (OBL):** Plant species that occur almost always
  (> 99% of the time) in wetlands; their dominance is the strongest
  evidence for hydrophytic vegetation.
- **Ordinary high water mark (OHWM):** The line on the shore
  established by the fluctuations of water leaving physical
  characteristics such as a clear natural line impressed on the bank,
  shelving, destruction of terrestrial vegetation, or presence of
  litter and debris; used to define the lateral extent of jurisdictional
  waters.
- **Problem area:** A site where one or more of the three wetland
  criteria are not clearly met or where atypical conditions (drought,
  altered hydrology, recent disturbance) complicate standard
  application of the three-parameter approach; requires additional
  documentation and may require a USACE district determination.
- **Sample plot (data point):** A defined area (typically 5 m radius
  for vegetation; a single soil pit for soils; a 10 m radius for
  hydrology indicators) within which all three wetland criteria are
  assessed together.
- **Upland:** An area that does not meet one or more of the three
  required wetland criteria; not subject to Section 404 jurisdiction.
- **Wetland boundary:** The line on the landscape separating areas that
  meet all three wetland criteria from areas that do not; the primary
  product of a wetland delineation.
- **Wetland indicator status (WIS):** A USACE classification of plant
  species by their probability of occurrence in wetlands: OBL
  (obligate wetland), FACW (facultative wetland), FAC (facultative),
  FACU (facultative upland), UPL (upland). Current designations are
  maintained by the USACE National Wetland Plant List (NWPL).


## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Unstable substrates (soft muck, quicksand-like
  conditions in saturated soils); risk of sinking, tripping on
  submerged debris, or falling. Standing water may conceal holes and
  channels.
- **Biological:** Mosquitoes (disease vectors including West Nile
  virus), ticks (Lyme disease, RMSF), venomous snakes, poison
  oak/ivy (*Toxicodendron* spp.), stinging nettles, and waterborne
  pathogens. Avoid direct skin contact with standing water.
- **Environmental:** Heat stress in summer; hypothermia in winter and
  spring. Wetlands offer little shade in open marsh environments.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Rubber boots or chest waders (knee boots minimum)
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (for soil pit work)
- [ ] Long sleeves and long pants (tick and mosquito protection)
- [ ] Insect repellent (DEET or picaridin)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen SPF 30+)
- [ ] Personal flotation device (if water depth exceeds knee level or
      if working from a watercraft)

### Emergency Procedures

Work in pairs at minimum. If a team member becomes stuck in soft
substrate, distribute weight on a board, backpack, or rope and pull
laterally rather than vertically. Refer to
[SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).

## Estimated Time

| Task                                         | Time (2-person crew)        |
|:---------------------------------------------|:----------------------------|
| Office pre-work (maps, records, NWPL lookup) | 2--4 hours                  |
| Site reconnaissance walk                     | 30--60 minutes              |
| Sample plot assessment (per plot)            | 15--30 minutes              |
| Boundary flagging and GPS waypoints          | 1--2 hours per 100 m boundary|
| Field data compilation                       | 30--60 minutes              |
| Office post-work (report, map, data entry)   | 4--8 hours                  |


## Procedure

### Step 1: Pre-Field Office Work

Before entering the field, complete the following:

1. Obtain and review available information:
   - USFWS National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) maps
     ([fws.gov/wetlands](https://www.fws.gov/wetlands/))
   - USDA Web Soil Survey (websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov) -- note mapped
     hydric soils and map unit descriptions
   - USGS topographic maps (7.5-minute quadrangles)
   - Aerial/satellite imagery (Google Earth historical layers) --
     look for inundation signatures, dark organic soils, and
     characteristic vegetation patterns
   - NOAA precipitation records for the region to assess whether
     current year is a drought, normal, or wet year (relevant to
     atypical situation determinations)

2. Generate a base map at a scale appropriate for the site
   (1:2,400 for small sites; 1:4,800 for large sites). Include
   NWI polygons, soil map unit boundaries, topographic contours,
   and property boundaries.

3. Look up current wetland indicator status (WIS) for all plant
   species expected at the site on the USACE National Wetland Plant
   List ([plants.usace.army.mil](https://plants.usace.army.mil)).

4. Identify the appropriate USACE district and confirm whether a
   preliminary jurisdictional determination (PJD) or approved
   jurisdictional determination (AJD) is ultimately required.

### Step 2: Site Reconnaissance

On arrival at the field site, conduct a reconnaissance walk before
placing any sample plots:

1. Walk the entire site perimeter and any internal drainages or basins
   to develop a mental model of landscape position, drainage patterns,
   and vegetation transitions.
2. Identify probable wetland areas (standing or ponded water, dark
   organic soils visible at surface, wet-adapted vegetation) and
   probable upland areas (well-drained soils, upland vegetation).
3. Identify any obvious disturbances (ditching, filling, altered
   hydrology, grazing, invasive species) that could create problem
   areas.
4. Note the approximate location of vegetation transitions, which
   are often close to the wetland boundary.
5. Sketch a rough site map with probable wetland/upland zones and
   planned transect routes.

### Step 3: Establish Transects and Sample Plots

1. Establish transects perpendicular to the suspected wetland
   boundary, spaced to adequately characterize the site. For
   EA Program sites, transects are typically spaced 25--50 m apart;
   closer spacing is used in complex or small-scale boundaries.

2. On each transect, place sample plots at:
   - A clearly wetland location (well within the apparent wetland)
   - A clearly upland location (well outside the apparent wetland)
   - One or more locations straddling the suspected boundary

3. Flag each sample plot center with flagging tape and record GPS
   coordinates. Use a consistent color for wetland plots and a
   different color for upland plots.

4. Number all sample plots sequentially and record them on the
   base map.

### Step 4: Assess Hydrophytic Vegetation

At each sample plot (approximately 5 m radius), assess vegetation
in all strata present (tree, shrub/sapling, herb, woody vine):

1. List all plant species in each stratum. Identify to species level
   using regional keys (*Jepson Manual* for California).

2. Estimate percent areal cover for each species within each stratum
   to the nearest 5--10%.

3. For each species, record the current wetland indicator status (WIS)
   from the USACE NWPL for the Arid West region.

4. Determine dominant species in each stratum using the **50/20 rule**:

   a. Rank species within each stratum by decreasing percent cover.
   b. Add species from highest to lowest cover until the cumulative
      cover total reaches 50% or more of the total stratum cover.
   c. Include one additional species if it contributes at least 20%
      of the total stratum cover.
   d. All species added in steps (b) and (c) are dominant species
      for that stratum.

5. Tally the number of dominant species that are OBL, FACW, or FAC
   (hydrophytic) and the number that are FACU or UPL (upland).

6. The **hydrophytic vegetation criterion is met** if more than 50% of
   the dominant species across all strata are OBL, FACW, or FAC.

::: {.callout-note}
### FAC-Neutral Test

In borderline cases where FAC species are dominant, apply the
FAC-neutral test: exclude all FAC species and recalculate dominance
using only OBL, FACW, FACU, and UPL species. If the remaining
dominants are predominantly hydrophytic, the criterion is still met.
The FAC-neutral test is described in the Arid West Regional Supplement
[@usace2010regional].
:::

### Step 5: Assess Hydric Soils

At each sample plot, excavate a soil pit to at least 50 cm depth
(or to the water table or bedrock, whichever is shallower):

1. Excavate with a sharpshooter spade. If the pit fills with water,
   record the depth to water table and excavate no deeper.

2. Describe the soil profile using the form in Appendix A:
   - Horizon designation (A, B, C), depth (cm), and thickness
   - Munsell color (matrix and mottles/redoximorphic features) per
     [SOP-F405](SOP-F405-soil-color-munsell.qmd) -- record moist
     colors only
   - Texture (field ribbon test; see [SOP-F401](SOP-F401-soil-texture.qmd))
   - Structure, consistence, roots

3. Check for USDA NRCS Field Indicators of Hydric Soils (Version 8.2
   or current). For the Western Mountains, Valleys, and Coast (WMVC)
   region, the most applicable indicators include:

   | Indicator Code | Name                          | Key Feature                                   |
   |:---------------|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
   | A1             | Histosol                      | Organic soil (Oi, Oe, or Oa horizon > 40 cm) |
   | A2             | Histic epipedon               | Organic surface layer 20--40 cm               |
   | A3             | Black histic                  | Black (10YR 2/1) organic layer >= 20 cm       |
   | A11            | Depleted below dark surface   | Dark A over low-chroma (chroma <= 2) matrix   |
   | F2             | Loamy gleyed matrix           | Gley hue matrix in loamy soils                |
   | F3             | Depleted matrix               | > 60% low-chroma (chroma <= 2) matrix         |
   | F6             | Redox dark surface            | Dark A over depleted or reduced matrix        |
   | F8             | Redox depressions             | Redox concentrations in depressions           |

4. The **hydric soil criterion is met** if one or more applicable
   field indicators are present at the appropriate depth. For most
   indicators in the Arid West Supplement, this means within the
   upper 30 cm of the soil profile [@usace2010regional].

::: {.callout-warning}
### Problematic Hydric Soil Situations

Soils in the Arid West may have low-chroma colors from parent material
(e.g., some shales, volcanic tuffs) rather than from saturation. If
in doubt, check for redox concentrations (bright orange/red Fe masses)
as corroborating evidence, and note the soil series and parent material
from Web Soil Survey.
:::

### Step 6: Assess Wetland Hydrology

At each sample plot, document evidence of wetland hydrology. The
USACE defines wetland hydrology as saturation within 30 cm of the
surface for a continuous period of at least 5% of the growing season
[@usace1987; @usace2010regional].

1. Record depth to surface water or saturated soil (standing water
   in the pit).

2. Check for **primary hydrology indicators** (in order of reliability):

   | Indicator                         | Description                                        |
   |:----------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
   | Surface water                     | Standing water present at time of visit            |
   | High water table                  | Water within 30 cm of surface in soil pit          |
   | Saturation                        | Saturated soil within 30 cm (water oozes when squeezed) |

3. Check for **secondary hydrology indicators** (two or more required
   when primary indicators are absent):

   | Indicator                         | Description                                        |
   |:----------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
   | Water marks                       | Staining on tree trunks or structures              |
   | Sediment deposits                 | Fresh mineral sediment on leaves or stems          |
   | Drift lines                       | Lines of debris deposited by receding water        |
   | Waterlogged soils                 | Confirmed by soil pit; no free water but saturated |
   | Water-stained leaves              | Grayish-brown discoloration of litter              |
   | Oxidized rhizospheres             | Orange halos around living roots in grey matrix    |
   | FAC-neutral plant communities     | Vegetation dominance by OBL/FACW species           |
   | Crayfish burrows                  | Chimney mounds indicating seasonal saturation      |

4. For arid-region sites, pay particular attention to oxidized
   rhizospheres (a primary indicator in the Arid West Supplement) and
   drift/wrack lines along swales and basins.

5. The **wetland hydrology criterion is met** if at least one primary
   indicator is present, or at least two secondary indicators are
   present, at the time of visit; or if the site has documented
   evidence of seasonal or periodic inundation from well records or
   gauges (see [SOP-F306](SOP-F306-wetland-hydrology-monitoring.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note}
### Arid-Region Hydrology Timing

At arid and semi-arid sites, surface water and high water tables may
only be present during a brief seasonal window. When conducting
delineations outside the wet season, rely on secondary indicators
and, where available, water level logger data from monitoring wells.
Document the date of the visit and regional precipitation conditions
in all field data sheets. See [SOP-F306](SOP-F306-wetland-hydrology-monitoring.qmd)
for long-term hydrology monitoring methods.
:::

### Step 7: Apply the Three-Parameter Test

At each sample plot, compile results from Steps 4--6:

1. Record whether each of the three criteria is met (yes/no) on
   the field data sheet (Appendix A).

2. **A sample plot is classified as wetland if and only if all three
   criteria are met.** If any criterion is absent, the plot is
   classified as upland (or a transitional/problem area if two of
   three are met).

3. If two of three criteria are met, flag the plot as a potential
   **problem area** and document the specific conditions. Common
   problem area types include:
   - Recently disturbed wetlands (vegetation removed, soil disturbed)
   - Drought-year assessments (hydrology not apparent)
   - Altered hydrology (ditched, drained, or impounded areas)
   - Atypical vegetation (recent burn, mowing, herbicide)

4. For problem areas, apply the appropriate USACE atypical situation
   procedures as described in the Regional Supplement
   [@usace2010regional].

### Step 8: Flag and Map the Wetland Boundary

1. Between each pair of adjacent wetland and upland sample plots on
   a transect, locate the wetland boundary by walking perpendicular
   to the transect and reassessing the three criteria at intermediate
   points until the line of change is identified.

2. Flag the wetland boundary with a distinct color (use a third color
   different from the wetland and upland plot flags). Place flags
   every 5--10 m or at every change in direction.

3. Record GPS waypoints at each boundary flag using
   [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd). Waypoint naming
   convention: `WB_[transect]-[sequence]` (e.g., `WB_T1-01`).

4. Photograph the boundary flags from multiple angles; include a
   scale bar (person or measuring tape) in at least one photo per
   transect.

5. Sketch the boundary on the field base map, noting all sample plot
   locations and transect lines.

### Step 9: Field Quality Review

Before leaving the site, complete the following checks:

- [ ] All sample plots have GPS coordinates recorded
- [ ] Every plot has complete data for all three criteria
- [ ] All boundary flags are GPS-logged
- [ ] At least two representative photographs per sample plot
- [ ] Boundary is continuous between all transects (no gaps)
- [ ] Problem areas are flagged and documented
- [ ] Equipment has been decontaminated per
      [SOP-F007](SOP-F007-field-decontamination.qmd)

### Step 10: Post-Field Office Work

1. Enter all field data into the project database within 48 hours
   per [SOP-L803](../lab_sops/SOP-L803-data-entry-database.qmd).

2. Import GPS waypoints and generate a georeferenced boundary map in
   GIS software (see [SOP-L804](../lab_sops/SOP-L804-gis-spatial-data.qmd)).

3. Overlay the delineated boundary on aerial imagery, NWI maps,
   and soil survey maps to check for consistency; note and document
   any discrepancies.

4. Calculate wetland area (hectares) from the GIS boundary polygon.

5. Compile the delineation report with:
   - Site description and location map
   - Methods summary (reference to this SOP)
   - Summary table of all sample plots and three-parameter results
   - Wetland boundary map
   - Photographs
   - Conclusions regarding jurisdictional status
   - Any problem areas and how they were addressed

6. Archive all raw field data sheets (scanned), GPS track files, GIS
   shapefiles, and the final report per project data management
   protocols.


## Quality Control

- A minimum of two observers must conduct the vegetation assessment
  at each sample plot; independent species lists must be reconciled
  before leaving the plot.
- Munsell color readings must be made by two observers and must agree
  within one value and one chroma step; discrepancies require a
  consensus re-read per [SOP-F405](SOP-F405-soil-color-munsell.qmd).
- GPS boundary waypoints must be collected with horizontal accuracy
  < 3 m (WAAS-enabled or equivalent). Record DOP and fix type.
- At 10% of sample plots, return the following day and re-assess the
  hydrophytic vegetation criterion independently; dominant species
  lists must agree within 10 percentage points cover.
- Final delineation maps must be reviewed by the PI before submission
  to any regulatory agency or inclusion in project reports.


## Data Management

1. Raw field data sheets must be scanned and uploaded to the project
   folder within 48 hours of fieldwork.
2. Enter tabular sample plot data into the project database using the
   standardized template in Appendix B.
3. GPS tracks and waypoints must be exported and backed up immediately
   on return from the field.
4. All GIS boundary files must be saved in both shapefile and GeoJSON
   formats and versioned in the project Git repository.
5. Version-control all analysis scripts and report documents per
   [SOP-L801](../lab_sops/SOP-L801-rstudio-github.qmd).

## Training Record

Before conducting wetland delineations independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP, [SOP-F001](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd),
   [SOP-F306](SOP-F306-wetland-hydrology-monitoring.qmd), and
   [SOP-F405](SOP-F405-soil-color-munsell.qmd) in full
2. Review the USACE 1987 Manual and Arid West Regional Supplement
   [@usace1987; @usace2010regional]
3. Complete at least one supervised delineation transect, including
   independent application of the 50/20 rule and hydric soil field
   indicators, with results reviewed by the PI
4. Demonstrate Munsell color reading proficiency per
   [SOP-F405](SOP-F405-soil-color-munsell.qmd) inter-observer
   calibration requirements
5. Successfully enter and map a practice delineation dataset in GIS
6. Be signed off by the PI or field lead

## Appendix C: Wetland Indicator Status Quick Reference {.appendix}

| Code | Category             | Wetland Occurrence | Delineation Implication              |
|:-----|:---------------------|:-------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| OBL  | Obligate wetland     | > 99%              | Strong evidence for hydrophytic veg  |
| FACW | Facultative wetland  | 67--99%            | Evidence for hydrophytic veg         |
| FAC  | Facultative          | 34--66%            | Equivocal; apply FAC-neutral test    |
| FACU | Facultative upland   | 1--33%             | Evidence against hydrophytic veg     |
| UPL  | Upland               | < 1%               | Strong evidence against hydrophytic veg |

Current WIS designations for the Arid West region are available at
